CHAPTER XLIV

Experienced women are not frightened when a woman faints, or do they
hastily attribute it to anything but physical causes, which they have
often seen produce it. Catherine bustled about; laid the girl down with
her head on the floor quite flat, opened the window, and unloosed her
dress as she lay. Not till she had done all this did she step to the
door and say, rather loudly:

“Come here, if you please.”

Margaret Van Eyck and Reicht came, and found Margaret lying quite flat,
and Catherine beating her hands.

“Oh, my poor girl! What have you done to her?”

“Me?” said Catherine angrily.

“What has happened, then?”

“Nothing, madam; nothing more than is natural in her situation.”

Margaret Van Eyck coloured with ire.

“You do well to speak so coolly,” said she, “you that are the cause of
her situation.”

“That I am not,” said Catherine bluntly; “nor any woman born.”

“What! was it not you and your husband that kept them apart? and now he
has gone to Italy all alone. Situation indeed! You have broken her heart
amongst you.”

“Why, madam? Who is it then? in Heaven's name! To hear you, one would
think this was my Gerard's lass. But that can't be. This fur never cost
less than five crowns the ell; besides, this young gentlewoman is a
wife; or ought to be.”

“Of course she ought. And who is the cause she is none? Who came before
them at the very altar?”

“God forgive them, whoever it was,” said Catherine gravely; “me it was
not, nor my man.”

“Well,” said the other, a little softened, “now you have seen her,
perhaps you will not be quite so bitter against her madam. She is coming
to, thank Heaven.”

“Me bitter against her?” said Catherine; “no, that is all over. Poor
soul! trouble behind her and trouble afore her; and to think of my
setting her, of all living women, to read Gerard's letter to me. Ay, and
that was what made her go off, I'll be sworn. She is coming to. What,
sweetheart! be not afeard, none are here but friends.”

They seated her in an easy chair. As the colour was creeping back to her
face and lips. Catherine drew Margaret Van Eyck aside.

“Is she staying with you, if you please?”

“No, madam.”

“I wouldn't let her go back to Sevenbergen to-night, then.”

“That is as she pleases. She still refuses to bide the night.”

“Ay, but you are older than she is; you can make her. There, she is
beginning to notice.”

Catherine then put her mouth to Margaret Van Eyck's ear for half a
moment; it did not seem time enough to whisper a word, far less a
sentence. But on some topics females can flash communication to female
like lightning, or thought itself.

The old lady started, and whispered back--

“It's false! it is a calumny! it is monstrous! look at her face. It is
blasphemy to accuse such a face.”

“Tut! tut! tut!” said the other; “you might as well say this is not my
hand. I ought to know; and I tell ye it is so.”

Then, much to Margaret Van Eyck's surprise, she went up to the girl, and
taking her round the neck, kissed her warmly.

“I suffered for Gerard, and you shed your blood for him I do hear; his
own words show me that I have been to blame, the very words you have
read to me. Ay, Gerard, my child, I have held aloof from her; but I'll
make it up to her once I begin. You are my daughter from this hour.”

Another warm embrace sealed this hasty compact, and the woman of impulse
was gone.

Margaret lay back in her chair, and a feeble smile stole over her face.
Gerard's mother had kissed her and called her daughter; but the next
moment she saw her old friend looking at her with a vexed air.

“I wonder you let that woman kiss you.”

“His mother!” murmured Margaret, half reproachfully.

“Mother, or no mother, you would not let her touch you if you knew what
she whispered in my ear about you.”

“About me?” said Margaret faintly.

“Ay, about you, whom she never saw till to-night.” The old lady was
proceeding, with some hesitation and choice of language, to make
Margaret share her indignation, when an unlooked-for interruption closed
her lips.

The young woman slid from her chair to her knees, and began to pray
piteously to her for pardon. From the words and the manner of her
penitence a bystander would have gathered she had inflicted some cruel
wrong, some intolerable insult, upon her venerable friend.

Catherine moved swiftly and with purpose: she laid the girl down flat on the floor, her head resting low, opened the window wide to let in fresh air, and loosened the tight folds of her dress as she lay still. Only after all this did she step to the door and call out, her voice firm and clear: “Come here, if you please.”

Margaret Van Eyck and Reicht entered at once, finding the young woman lying motionless, while Catherine stood beside her, hands clenched in quiet distress. “Oh, my poor child!” exclaimed Margaret Van Eyck. “What has happened to her?”

“Me?” Catherine replied sharply. “What could I possibly have done?”

“Nothing, madam,” said the other gently, “nothing beyond what is natural given her circumstances.”

A flush rose in Margaret Van Eyck’s cheeks. “You speak so calmly,” she said, “when it was your actions that brought her to this state.”

“That I am not,” Catherine answered bluntly, “nor any woman alive.”

“Was it not you and your husband who kept them apart? And now he has gone to Italy alone—no wife by his side. This is no mere circumstance. You’ve broken her heart between you.”

“Why, madam,” Catherine returned, “who then? In Heaven’s name! To hear you talk, one would think this were Gerard’s own sweetheart. But that cannot be. Look at this fur—five crowns an ell, and more than that in quality. Besides, this young lady is a married woman—or ought to be.”

“Of course she ought,” Margaret Van Eyck replied. “And who is to blame that she isn’t? Who stepped forward before them at the very altar?”

“God forgive whoever it was,” Catherine said gravely, “but it was not I, nor my husband.”

“Well,” the older woman conceded, her tone softening slightly, “now you’ve seen her, perhaps you won’t be so harsh toward her. Thank God, she is coming round.”

“Me bitter against her?” Catherine asked, surprised. “No, that is over. Poor soul—trouble behind her, trouble ahead. And yet I sent her, of all people, to read Gerard’s letter to me. That must have been it—she fainted from the weight of it. She is stirring now. Come, sweetheart—don’t be afraid. There’s no one here but friends.”

They helped her into a comfortable chair. As color slowly returned to her face and lips, Catherine drew Margaret Van Eyck aside. “Will she stay with you tonight?” she asked quietly.

“No, madam,” came the reply.

“I wouldn’t let her return to Sevenbergen tonight,” Catherine insisted.

“It is her choice,” Margaret Van Eyck said firmly. “She still refuses to remain.”

“But you are older than she,” Catherine pressed. “You can insist. See—she is beginning to notice.”

Then, without speaking aloud, Catherine leaned close and whispered something into the other woman’s ear—so briefly that it seemed impossible even a word could pass. Yet between two women such as these, silence could carry more meaning than words. The old lady started visibly, then whispered back, trembling: “It’s false! It’s slander! It’s monstrous! Look at her face—how could anyone accuse such a face?”

“Tut! tut! tut!” Catherine snapped. “You might as well say this is not my hand. I know it well—and I tell you plainly, it is true.”

To Margaret Van Eyck’s astonishment, Catherine then approached the girl, took her in her arms, and kissed her warmly upon the cheek. “I suffered for Gerard,” she said, “and you shed your blood for him—I heard his own words. He told me plainly I had wronged her. Yes, Gerard, my child, I held back from her; but from this hour, I will make amends. You are my daughter now.”

A second embrace sealed their sudden bond, and the impulsive woman turned away, leaving the room.

Margaret sank back into her chair, a fragile smile playing across her lips. Gerard’s mother had kissed her and called her daughter. But in the next breath, she saw her dear friend watching her with a look of deep disapproval.

“I wonder you allowed that woman to touch you,” the elder said, sternly.

“His mother,” Margaret murmured, half in reproach.

“Mother or not,” the other replied, “you would not let her near you if you knew what she whispered to me about you.”

“About me?” Margaret whispered, pale again.

“Yes—about you, whom she never saw until tonight.”

Margaret Van Eyck began to speak, choosing her words carefully, eager to share her outrage—but before she could go further, a sudden interruption silenced her.

The young woman slid from her chair onto her knees, bowing her head in anguish. With trembling voice and tear-filled eyes, she began to beg for forgiveness—not for herself, but for the pain she had caused. Her sorrow was so deep, her humility so complete, that any observer would have believed she had committed some terrible injustice, some unbearable insult, against the noble woman before her.
